books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — Theodore Roosevelt and the 'Square Deal'
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: Theodore Roosevelt, speech to farmers, New York (1903)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20; verbatim excerpt (abridged) from Theodore Roosevelt's 1903 speech, public domain.
stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20: In 1902, anthracite coal miners went on strike, and President Theodore Roosevelt called both sides to the White House, threatening to take over the mines if the owners would not negotiate. The miners won a 10 percent wage increase but not union recognition. Roosevelt called the settlement a 'Square Deal.' He also used the Sherman Antitrust Act against the Northern Securities Company, a railroad holding company, and in 1904 the Supreme Court upheld the breakup.

'We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. ... We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.' — Theodore Roosevelt, speech to farmers in New York, 1903 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: Roosevelt's handling of the 1902 coal strike showed that he believed government should

options.text: always side with the business owners
options.misconception: Roosevelt threatened to take over the mines if owners would not negotiate; that is not siding with owners.

options.text: act as a referee between labor and business
always side with the striking workers
options.misconception: The miners won a raise but not union recognition; Roosevelt did not give labor everything it asked.

options.text: stay out of labor disputes entirely, as earlier presidents had
options.misconception: Roosevelt intervened directly, calling both sides to the White House; staying out was the old Gilded Age approach.

rationales.A: Roosevelt pressured the owners to negotiate and threatened a takeover. That is not siding with business.
rationales.B: Roosevelt brought both sides to the White House, pressed the owners to negotiate, and gave the miners a raise without union recognition. That is a referee's settlement: neither side gets everything, and government keeps the peace.
rationales.C: The miners did not win union recognition. A president who always sided with labor would have given it to them.
rationales.D: Roosevelt did the opposite of staying out. He called both sides to the White House and set the terms.
rationales.general:
1. Watch what Roosevelt did. He called owners and miners to the White House and threatened to take over the mines.
2. Watch the result. Miners got a 10 percent raise, owners kept the union out: a split decision.
3. Name the role. A president who splits the difference between labor and business is acting as a referee.
Remember: a settlement's shape reveals the president's role, so read who got what before naming it.
